- When sentiment is consistently low or negative (e.g., < 0.3) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; adjust forecast downward by 2–5%.
- If model shows steady upward trend with no volatility, and true outcome has sharp spikes or drops, reduce forecast slope and add volatility buffer.
- After a large spike in true price, model often overshoots and continues upward; cap forecast at 1–2% above recent peak or use mean-reversion anchor.
- If sentiment is high (e.g., > 0.7) and model is flat or slightly rising, consider downward bias — reduce forecast by 1–3% to avoid overconfidence.
- For 30-day horizon, if true outcome deviates > 5% from model in first 5–7 days, apply “early correction” — adjust first 5–7 forecast points downward by 1–3% based on sentiment decay.
- If sentiment history shows rapid shift from negative to positive, model often fails to react — delay forecast adjustment until sentiment stabilizes or exceeds 0.6.
- Mean reversion is strong in 30-day horizon when true outcome deviates > 10% from 14-day moving average — apply correction toward that average, especially if sentiment is neutral or slightly negative.
